\chapter{Doctor, Pills and Tiredness}
\label{ch:doctor-pastilla-cansado}
\hlchaptermodality{408}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can identify a doctor, a medicinal tablet and the state of being tired.}

Retrieve three health words across appointment, medicine and state messages.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[el doctor / la doctora]{el doctor / la doctora — the teacher-word at the clinic}

\label{lesson:ES-C408-doctor}



\begin{quote}
Recall \textbf{el médico}, the physician. Spanish has another word you will hear when making an appointment: \textbf{el doctor} or \textbf{la doctora}.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
Medieval Latin \textbf{doctor} meant “teacher,” from \textbf{docēre}, “to teach.” English kept the same academic word. Spanish also uses \textbf{doctor} for a physician and as a form of address. That does not erase the older academic meaning: context tells you whether the doctor holds a doctorate or is treating a patient.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: name the person}]
The ending follows the person: \textbf{el doctor}, \textbf{la doctora}. To ask for an appointment, use the frame \textbf{pedir cita con el doctor}. \textbf{Médico} remains the more specific profession-word; \textbf{doctor} is the word the mock message uses.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el doctor}
  \item \emph{la doctora}
  \item \emph{una cita con el doctor}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Doctor? (\emph{El doctor; la doctora}.)

Source: \href{https://dle.rae.es/doctor}{DLE: doctor}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la pastilla]{la pastilla — a small formed portion}

\label{lesson:ES-C408-pastilla}



\begin{quote}
You have an appointment with \textbf{el doctor}. The next message names what you take: \textbf{la pastilla}.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{Pastilla} belongs transparently with \textbf{pasta} and the small-form ending \textbf{-illa}: a little formed portion. The older physical idea survives in a bar of soap or a mint. In the clinic, \textbf{una pastilla} is a small medicinal tablet.

Do not overtranslate the shape. In this health frame, \textbf{pastilla} means the pill or tablet, not pasta to eat.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la pastilla}
  \item \emph{una pastilla}
  \item \emph{el doctor y la pastilla}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Pill or tablet? (\emph{La pastilla}.)

Sources: \href{https://dle.rae.es/pastilla}{DLE: pastilla}; \href{https://webfrl.rae.es/BRAE\_DB\_PDF/TOMO\_V/XXIII/Alemany\_333\_349.pdf}{RAE, derivation and composition: \emph{pastilla} from \emph{pasta}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
